evidence.claim: Articles 72-75 make the Prime Minister the Cabinet's representative who submits bills, reports on foreign relations, and exercises control and supervision over administrative branches; the Cabinet conducts foreign affairs, concludes treaties with Diet approval, prepares the budget, and laws and cabinet orders are signed by the competent minister and countersigned by the Prime Minister.
evidence.title: The Constitution of Japan
evidence.excerpt: Articles 72-75 make the Prime Minister the Cabinet's representative who submits bills, reports on foreign relations, and exercises control and supervision over administrative branches; the Cabinet conducts foreign affairs, concludes treaties with Diet approval, prepares the budget, and laws and cabinet orders are signed by the competent minister and countersigned by the Prime Minister.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Authoritative constitutional text from the official legal translation site; stable baseline for office powers.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Defines Kishida's office-level authority and constraints rather than a ruler-specific act.
contrary_evidence: Text does not show informal coalition limits or day-to-day bargaining constraints.

evidence.claim: The government stated that it would not discuss 'nuclear sharing,' would maintain the three non-nuclear principles, and viewed nuclear energy as restricted to peaceful purposes; it said Japan's stance had not changed.
evidence.title: 書面による質問に対する回答
evidence.excerpt: The government stated that it would not discuss 'nuclear sharing,' would maintain the three non-nuclear principles, and viewed nuclear energy as restricted to peaceful purposes; it said Japan's stance had not changed.
evidence.source_locator: Written response on nuclear sharing / three non-nuclear principles
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official cabinet response on the prime minister's own website; direct record of policy stance.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida government stance against proliferation and hosting U.S. nuclear weapons.
contrary_evidence: Extended deterrence and alliance consultation remained in place, so this was a rejection of hosting/sharing rather than a broader disarmament breakthrough.

evidence.claim: Kishida and Secretary-General Guterres agreed to coordinate closely so the NPT Review Conference could produce a meaningful outcome, and Kishida pledged a $10 million contribution to establish a UN 'Youth Leader Fund' for a world without nuclear weapons.
evidence.title: Prime Minister Kishida’s Meeting with United Nations Secretary-General Guterres
evidence.excerpt: Kishida and Secretary-General Guterres agreed to coordinate closely so the NPT Review Conference could produce a meaningful outcome, and Kishida pledged a $10 million contribution to establish a UN 'Youth Leader Fund' for a world without nuclear weapons.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official diplomatic record with date, participants, and specific funding pledge.
evidence.period_fit: Immediate follow-through on the August NPT trip
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida institution-building and external coordination choice.
contrary_evidence: A funding pledge is indirect; it supports institutions but does not itself change arsenals or command doctrine.

evidence.claim: Kishida said Japan would uphold the Three Non-Nuclear Principles and keep working toward a world without nuclear weapons, while stressing transparency, further nuclear arms reductions, and non-proliferation.
evidence.title: Address by Prime Minister KISHIDA Fumio at the Nagasaki Peace Memorial Ceremony
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said Japan would uphold the Three Non-Nuclear Principles and keep working toward a world without nuclear weapons, while stressing transparency, further nuclear arms reductions, and non-proliferation.
evidence.source_locator: Middle paragraphs beginning 'Japan will walk decisively forward...'
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official ceremony address by the prime minister on the PM website.
evidence.period_fit: Directly after the NPT conference and during the 2022 nuclear-crisis cycle
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida public commitment on nuclear restraint and disarmament.
contrary_evidence: Ceremonial language is not the same as implementation or treaty change.

evidence.claim: Kishida said the NPT Review Conference failed to adopt an outcome document because of Russia's opposition, called that result extremely regrettable, and said Japan would continue realistic efforts in line with the Hiroshima Action Plan.
evidence.title: Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida on His Reaction to the Outcome of the Review Conference of the Parties to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) and Other Matters
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said the NPT Review Conference failed to adopt an outcome document because of Russia's opposition, called that result extremely regrettable, and said Japan would continue realistic efforts in line with the Hiroshima Action Plan.
evidence.source_locator: Opening response on the conference outcome and the TPNW follow-up
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official response immediately after the conference on the PM website.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida assessment of the setback and continuation strategy.
contrary_evidence: The statement does not show that Kishida could overcome the diplomatic deadlock; it also highlights the limits of Japan's leverage.

evidence.claim: Japan's UN mission said that under Prime Minister Kishida's leadership, Japan would continue working with the international community toward a world without nuclear weapons, including through a UN General Assembly resolution, and warned that the possibility of nuclear weapon use was higher than at any time since the Cold War.
evidence.title: Statement by H.E. Ambassador ISHIKANE Kimihiro, Permanent Representative of Japan to the United Nations, at the High-level Plenary Meeting to Commemorate and Promote the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons
evidence.publisher: Permanent Mission of Japan to the United Nations
evidence.excerpt: Japan's UN mission said that under Prime Minister Kishida's leadership, Japan would continue working with the international community toward a world without nuclear weapons, including through a UN General Assembly resolution, and warned that the possibility of nuclear weapon use was higher than at any time since the Cold War.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official UN mission statement directly attributing the posture to Kishida's leadership.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Indirect but explicit attribution to Kishida's leadership line.
contrary_evidence: This is a diplomatic statement, not a verified policy outcome.

evidence.claim: Japan's draft resolution 'Steps to building a common roadmap towards a world without nuclear weapons' was adopted by the UN General Assembly with 147 votes and was explicitly based on Prime Minister Kishida's Hiroshima Action Plan, calling for continued non-use, transparency, and disarmament education.
evidence.title: The Adoption of the Draft Resolution on the Elimination of Nuclear Weapons submitted by Japan in the Plenary Meeting of the United Nations General Assembly
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan
evidence.excerpt: Japan's draft resolution 'Steps to building a common roadmap towards a world without nuclear weapons' was adopted by the UN General Assembly with 147 votes and was explicitly based on Prime Minister Kishida's Hiroshima Action Plan, calling for continued non-use, transparency, and disarmament education.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official foreign-ministry press release on the UN vote and the resolution's contents.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida-led diplomatic initiative and agenda imprint.
contrary_evidence: Resolution adoption is broad but still soft power; it does not bind nuclear states to disarm.

evidence.claim: The mayors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki thanked Kishida for attending the NPT Review Conference and announcing the Hiroshima Action Plan, but urged Japan to sign and ratify the TPNW and to attend future meetings as an observer.
evidence.title: Letter of Request to Prime Minister Kishida Regarding the TPNW
evidence.excerpt: The mayors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki thanked Kishida for attending the NPT Review Conference and announcing the Hiroshima Action Plan, but urged Japan to sign and ratify the TPNW and to attend future meetings as an observer.
evidence.source_locator: Letter body, especially the paragraphs on the TPNW and observer participation
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official local-government letter from the two atomic-bomb cities; strong critical/favorable pressure source.
evidence.period_fit: Immediate 2022 domestic criticism of Kishida's nuclear policy line
evidence.ruler_attribution: External criticism of Kishida's pace and treaty choices rather than a Kishida action.
contrary_evidence: The letter also explicitly recognizes his NPT attendance and Hiroshima Action Plan, so it is critical but not dismissive of his efforts.

unresolved_gaps: Stronger direct evidence of Kishida's personal control over police, prosecutors, and protective institutions before and after the Abe assassination.
More evidence that the church-scandal and protest responses reduced actual harm rather than only improving the public narrative.
More independent evidence that the 2022 growth/distribution package actually changed household welfare or investment outcomes rather than only announcing them.
Better separation of Kishida's policy effect from BOJ policy, exchange-rate moves, and imported inflation shocks.
Direct year-end outcome evidence for child, fertility, and social-service gains attributable to the 2022 package.
More subgroup evidence on single-parent households, disabled people, housing insecurity, and food insecurity.
Direct, traceable evidence of Kishida's own assets, private interests, donor links, or personal self-enrichment is missing.
Independent corroboration of the personal claim that Kishida had no links to the former Unification Church and that his vetting instructions were fully followed.
More independent evidence on whether the 2022 startup, digital, and green-growth agenda actually produced measurable execution, not just planning.
Clearer separation of Kishida's own execution from external shocks and inherited macro conditions when judging the economic package and wage trajectory.
